claim: NDE1 mutations cause brain developmental disorders
source: In this study, we show a novel function for NDE1, whose mutations cause brain developmental disorders, in safeguarding the genome through S phase during early steps of neural progenitor fate restrictive differentiation.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as an established fact about NDE1 mutations.

claim: Nde1 mutant neural progenitors showed catastrophic DNA double strand breaks concurrent with DNA replication
source: Nde1 mutant neural progenitors showed catastrophic DNA double strand breaks concurrent with the DNA replication.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: DNA damage in Nde1 mutants evoked DNA damage responses
source: This evoked DNA damage responses, led to the activation of p53-dependent apoptosis, and resulted in the reduction of neurons in cortical layer II/III.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data showing phosphorylation of p53 and H2AX.

claim: DNA damage in Nde1 mutants led to activation of p53-dependent apoptosis
source: This evoked DNA damage responses, led to the activation of p53-dependent apoptosis, and resulted in the reduction of neurons in cortical layer II/III.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by rescue experiments with p53 knockout.

claim: DNA damage in Nde1 mutants resulted in reduction of neurons in cortical layer II/III
source: This evoked DNA damage responses, led to the activation of p53-dependent apoptosis, and resulted in the reduction of neurons in cortical layer II/III.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by quantitative analysis of Cux1+ neurons.

claim: A nuclear pool of Nde1 exists
source: We discovered a nuclear pool of Nde1, identified the interaction of Nde1 with cohesin and its associated chromatin remodeler, and showed that stalled DNA replication in Nde1 mutants specifically occurred in mid-late S phase at heterochromatin domains.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by immunohistology and confocal microscopy.

claim: Nde1 interacts with cohesin
source: We discovered a nuclear pool of Nde1, identified the interaction of Nde1 with cohesin and its associated chromatin remodeler, and showed that stalled DNA replication in Nde1 mutants specifically occurred in mid-late S phase at heterochromatin domains.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiments.

claim: Nde1 interacts with a chromatin remodeler associated with cohesin
source: We discovered a nuclear pool of Nde1, identified the interaction of Nde1 with cohesin and its associated chromatin remodeler, and showed that stalled DNA replication in Nde1 mutants specifically occurred in mid-late S phase at heterochromatin domains.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation showing SNF2h interaction.

claim: Stalled DNA replication in Nde1 mutants specifically occurred in mid-late S phase at heterochromatin domains
source: We discovered a nuclear pool of Nde1, identified the interaction of Nde1 with cohesin and its associated chromatin remodeler, and showed that stalled DNA replication in Nde1 mutants specifically occurred in mid-late S phase at heterochromatin domains.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by IdU-CldU sequential labeling experiments.

claim: NDE1-mediated heterochromatin replication is indispensible for neuronal differentiation
source: These findings suggest that NDE1-mediated heterochromatin replication is indispensible for neuronal differentiation, and that the loss of NDE1 function may lead to genomic neurological disorders.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings presented in the study.

claim: Loss of NDE1 function may lead to genomic neurological disorders
source: These findings suggest that NDE1-mediated heterochromatin replication is indispensible for neuronal differentiation, and that the loss of NDE1 function may lead to genomic neurological disorders.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the findings and clinical associations.

claim: Successfully completing S phase ensures genome integrity
source: Successfully completing the S phase of each cell cycle ensures genome integrity.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Impediment of DNA replication can lead to DNA damage and genomic disorders
source: Impediment of DNA replication can lead to DNA damage and genomic disorders.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: S phase controls DNA synthesis and establishes epigenetic state that defines differentiation identity
source: The precise control of the DNA synthesis (S) phase of each cell division cycle warrants the faithful replication of the entire genome and at the same time establishes the epigenetic state that defines the differentiation identity of individual cells (McNairn and Gilbert, 2003; Nordman and Orr-Weaver, 2012).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to support it.

claim: Chromatin protein components are disassembled and re-assembled during S phase
source: Concurrent with genome duplication, the protein components of chromatin are disassembled and re-assembled throughout the S phase into higher order structures that characterize the specific gene expression status of daughter cells (Alabert and Groth, 2012; Budhavarapu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to support it.

claim: The amount of time neural progenitors spend in S phase is highly correlated to cell fate of cerebral cortical neural progenitor cells
source: S phase-mediated genome regulation is recently shown to be essential not only for rapid expansion of neural progenitor pool but also for neural differentiation, as the amount of time neural progenitors spend in S phase is highly correlated to the cell fate of cerebral cortical neural progenitor cells (Arai et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation to support it.

claim: Longer S phase appears more necessary for self renewing than neuron-producing cell cycles
source: Longer S phase appears more necessary for self renewing than neuron-producing cell cycles, suggesting an S phase specific quality control in maintaining the identity of neural progenitors before their terminal neurogenic division.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from prior research.

claim: Functional impairment of genes important for DNA metabolism frequently leads to brain developmental pathology
source: The importance of genome maintenance in corticogenesis is also underscored by large amounts of clinical and experimental observation, which have shown that the functional impairment of genes important for DNA metabolism frequently leads to brain developmental pathology (McKinnon, 2009; Ciccia and Elledge, 2010; Zeman and Cimprich, 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to support it.

claim: NDE1 was originally identified as the CNS specific partner of LIS1
source: It was originally identified as the central nervous system (CNS) specific partner of LIS1 (known as PAFAH1B1) (Feng et al., 2000), whose haploinsufficiency results in lissencephaly (smooth brain) (Reiner et al., 1993).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to support it.

claim: LIS1 haploinsufficiency results in lissencephaly
source: It was originally identified as the central nervous system (CNS) specific partner of LIS1 (known as PAFAH1B1) (Feng et al., 2000), whose haploinsufficiency results in lissencephaly (smooth brain) (Reiner et al., 1993).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation to support it.

claim: Homozygous mutations of NDE1 cause microlissencephaly with up to 90% reduction in brain mass
source: Homozygous mutations of NDE1 were found recently to cause microlissencephaly (small and smooth brain) with up to 90% reduction in brain mass, while the affected individuals showed normal development of non-CNS organs (Alkuraya et al., 2011; Bakircioglu et al., 2011; Guven et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to support it.

claim: Individuals with homozygous NDE1 mutations show normal development of non-CNS organs
source: Homozygous mutations of NDE1 were found recently to cause microlissencephaly (small and smooth brain) with up to 90% reduction in brain mass, while the affected individuals showed normal development of non-CNS organs (Alkuraya et al., 2011; Bakircioglu et al., 2011; Guven et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to support it.

claim: Copy number variants in the NDE1 locus associate with a wide spectrum of neuropsychiatric disorders
source: Moreover, copy number variants (CNVs) in the NDE1 locus are increasingly shown to associate with a wide spectrum of neuropsychiatric disorders with complex genetic traits (Ullmann et al., 2007; Hannes et al., 2009; Heinzen et al., 2010; Mefford et al., 2010; Nagamani et al., 2011; Tropeano et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to support it.

claim: Nde1 and Lis1 function synergistically in a dose-dependent manner in governing generation of late-born cortical neurons
source: Genetic epistasis studies in mice demonstrated that Nde1 and Lis1 function synergistically in a dose-dependent manner in governing the generation of late-born cortical neurons that comprise the upper cortical layers II and III.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from prior genetic studies.

claim: Layer II/III neurons were specifically reduced in both Nde1−/− and Nde1+/− Lis1+/− mice
source: Layer II/III neurons were found specifically reduced in both Nde1−/− and Nde1+/− Lis1+/− mice, and they were abolished almost completely in Nde1−/−Lis1+/− mice along with severe brain hypoplasia but insignificant change in the body size (Feng and Walsh, 2004; Pawlisz et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to support it.

claim: Layer II/III neurons are evolutionarily novel and undergo great expansion in mammalian evolution
source: Neurons in cortical upper layers are evolutionarily novel and undergo great expansion in mammalian evolution (DeFelipe et al., 2002; Molnar et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to support it.

claim: Layer II/III neurons are essential for cognitive functions including perception, emotion, attention, and memory
source: They are highly diverse projection neurons and essential for cognitive functions including perception, emotion, attention, and memory through making functional connections among various cortical areas and between the two cerebral hemispheres (DeFelipe et al., 2002; Fame et al., 2011; Greig et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to support it.

claim: A substantial number of cells in the neocortex of Nde1−/−Lis1+/− and Nde1−/− mutants showed abnormally high γH2AX immunosignals
source: A substantial number of cells in the neocortex of Nde1−/−Lis1+/− and Nde1−/− mutants showed abnormally high γH2AX immunosignals, a hallmark for DNA double strand breaks (DSBs) (Thiriet and Hayes, 2005; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunohistological data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: γH2AX is a hallmark for DNA double strand breaks
source: A substantial number of cells in the neocortex of Nde1−/−Lis1+/− and Nde1−/− mutants showed abnormally high γH2AX immunosignals, a hallmark for DNA double strand breaks (DSBs) (Thiriet and Hayes, 2005; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation to support it.

claim: γH2AX+ cells in Nde1 mutants were often co-stained by antibodies to cleaved caspase 3
source: While γH2AX foci associated with DNA replication were also widely detected in wild-type and mutant cortices, the γH2AX+ signals observed in the mutant were several orders of magnitude higher, showed pan-nuclear pattern, and were often co-stained by antibodies to cleaved caspase 3 (CC3), the marker for apoptosis.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunohistological data.

claim: γH2AX+ cells in Nde1 mutants were confined in the VZ
source: While apoptosis was wide-spread and observed in both CP neurons and ventricular zone (VZ) neural progenitors (Pawlisz et al., 2008), γH2AX+ cells were confined in the VZ (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunohistological data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: DNA damage in Nde1 mutants occurred prior to apoptosis
source: This suggested that DNA damage occurred prior to apoptosis and that apoptosis was one of the endpoints of DNA damage caused by Nde1 deficiency.
evidence: This is an inference based on the spatial distribution of γH2AX+ and CC3+ cells.

claim: In Nde1−/−Lis1+/− brain, γH2AX+ and CC3+ cells were detected as early as E10.5
source: In the Nde1−/−Lis1+/− brain, γH2AX+ and CC3+ cells were detected as early as the onset of neocortical neurogenesis at E10.5 (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunohistological data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: DNA damage and apoptosis in Nde1 mutant cortex peaked at E12.5
source: From E10.5 to E12.5, as more neural progenitors become fate restricted, both DNA damage and apoptosis in the Nde1 mutant cortex increased and peaked at E12.5.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by temporal analysis of immunohistological data.

claim: γH2AX and CC3 signals were absent in the mutant cortical hem at E12.5
source: While γH2AX and CC3 signals were at peak levels in the neocortex of Nde1−/−Lis1+/− and Nde1−/− brains at E12.5, they were absent in the mutant cortical hem, the highly proliferating but non-neurogenic hippocampus organizer (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunohistological data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: DNA damage and apoptosis in Nde1 mutants were associated with neural progenitor differentiation as opposed to proliferation
source: This suggested that DNA damage and apoptosis caused by Nde1 mutation were associated with neural progenitor differentiation as opposed to proliferation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the absence of phenotype in the proliferating but non-neurogenic cortical hem.

claim: γH2AX+ and CC3 signals in Nde1 mutants were correlated spatially with the presence and abundance of newborn neurons
source: In all cortical sections examined, γH2AX+ and CC3 signals were correlated spatially with the presence and abundance of newborn neurons (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunohistological data shown in Figure 1D and supplement.

claim: Nde1−/−Lis1+/− and Nde1−/− cells showed longer comet tails compared to Nde1+/− cells
source: Compared to cells from Nde1+/− embryos, more Nde1−/−Lis1+/− and Nde1−/− cells showed longer comet tails, indicating that loss of Nde1 function indeed resulted in an increase in DNA lesions in the developing cortex (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by comet assay data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: γH2AX and phospho-p53 Ser18 were co-activated in mutant neocortical neural progenitors
source: Double immunostaining of γH2AX and phospho p53 at Ser18 showed their co-activation in mutant neocortical neural progenitors (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunohistological data shown in Figure 2B,C.

claim: Many mutant cells showed elevated γH2AX and p-p53S18 but lacked DNA condensation and fragmentation
source: Many mutant cells showed elevated γH2AX and p-p53S18 but lacked DNA condensation and fragmentation, supporting that γH2AX and p53 activation in Nde1 mutants occurred prior to the programmed cell death (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The level of p53 S18 hyper-phosphorylation correlated to Nde1 gene dosage
source: We found that the level of p53 S18 hyper-phosphorylation correlated to Nde1 gene dosage as well as to the degree of brain malformations caused by Nde1 mutations (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Loss of Nde1 resulted in an elevated basal level of p53
source: Similarly, the loss of Nde1 resulted in an elevated basal level of p53, which is known to be low in healthy cells, supporting the DDR-mediated p53 activation.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunoblotting data.

claim: Loss of p53 abolished apoptosis in Nde1−/− progenitors
source: As expected, the loss of p53 abolished apoptosis in Nde1−/− progenitors and restored the size of the Nde1 mutant brain (Figure 3A,B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunohistological and brain weight data shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: The brain of Nde1−/−Trp53−/− double mutant mice was nearly the same as wild-type in both size and structure at weaning age
source: The brain of Nde1−/−Trp53−/− double mutant mice was found to be nearly the same as those of wild-type in both size and structure at the weaning age.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by brain weight and histological data.

claim: The thickness of layer II/III neurons was fully restored in Nde1−/−Trp53−/− brains
source: Histological and immunohistological analyses showed all anatomical features, especially the thickness of layer II/III neurons was fully restored (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by histological data shown in Figure 3C,D.

claim: The fraction of Cux1+ neurons in Nde1−/−Trp53−/− brains was at wild-type level
source: Quantitative analysis of the fraction of Cux1 immunolabeled upper layer projection neurons (with respect to total NeuN+ or NeuN+Cux1-neurons) in the Nde1−/−Trp53−/− double mutant brain indicated that they were at the wild-type-level (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by quantitative immunohistological data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Microcephaly and reduced layer II/III neurons in Nde1 mutant brains result from p53-dependent apoptosis elicited by DDR
source: These results demonstrate that microcephaly and reduced layer II/III neurons caused by the loss of Nde1 is a result of p53-dependent apoptosis elicited by DDR and that NDE1 is specifically essential for the genomic integrity of neurons that conduct higher order brain functions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the p53 rescue experiments.

claim: Active DSBs and DDR in Nde1−/− brain occurred in primary multipotent neural progenitors in the VZ
source: Consistent with an essential role of Nde1 in early neuronal fate restriction, we found that active DSBs and DDR in the Nde1−/− brain occurred in the primary multipotent neural progenitors in the VZ but was rarely detected in the intermediate neural progenitors of the sub-ventricular zone (SVZ), and not in the post-mitotic neurons in the CP (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunohistological data shown in Figure 4A and supplements.

claim: About 20% of γH2AX+ progenitors in Nde1 mutants were also BrdU+
source: After BrdU transient labeling, we found about 20% of γH2AX+ progenitors were also BrdU+ (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by BrdU labeling and immunohistological data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Co-immunostaining of γH2AX and PH3 failed to show cells with elevated γH2AX during mitosis
source: In contrast, co-immunostaining of γH2AX and phospho-histone H3 (PH3) failed to show cells with elevated γH2AX during mitosis (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunohistological data shown in Figure 4 supplement 1C.

claim: DNA damage in Nde1 mutants can occur during DNA replication
source: Because of the transient nature of both γH2AX and the BrdU pulse, these results demonstrate that DNA damage caused by Nde1 deficiency can occur during DNA replication.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the BrdU and γH2AX co-labeling experiments.

claim: The Ts of Nde1−/− progenitors was significantly longer than that of wild-type cells
source: Our data showed that the Ts of Nde1−/− progenitors was significantly longer than that of the wild-type cells (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by sequential IdU-BrdU labeling data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Many nuclei in Nde1 mutants that stopped incorporating BrdU remained in the S phase zone of the basal VZ
source: Furthermore, we also noticed that in both Nde1−/−Lis1+/− and Nde1−/− mutants, many nuclei that stopped incorporating BrdU (IdU+BrdU−) remained in the S phase zone of the basal VZ instead of descending apically as seen in the wild-type progenitors (Figure 4D, white arrows).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by sequential labeling data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Basally localized IdU+BrdU− nuclei in Nde1 mutants were not in G2/M phase
source: As the basally localized IdU+BrdU− nuclei in the mutant were not recognized in G2/M by PH3 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A), it suggested that these mutant cells might arrest in the basal S phase zone due to the stalled DNA replication.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunohistological data shown in Figure 4 supplement 2A.

claim: About 47.5% of γH2AX+ cells in Nde1 mutants were IdU+BrdU−
source: However, we observed that rather than progressing to mitosis, these cells remained stalled and that about half (47.5%) of the γH2AX+ cells were positively stained by antibodies to IdU but not to BrdU, indicating that S phase-stalled cells underwent DDR by activating γH2AX (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by triple immunostaining data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Nde1−/− progenitors failed to show a significant difference in early S phase population compared to wild-type
source: By quantitative comparison of IdU-CldU labeled progenitors in the cortical VZ of wild-type and Nde1−/− mutant, we failed to detect a significant difference in the early S phase population but found more mutant progenitors in mid to late S phase (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by quantitative analysis of IdU-CldU labeling shown in Figure 5A.

claim: More Nde1−/− progenitors were found in mid to late S phase compared to wild-type
source: By quantitative comparison of IdU-CldU labeled progenitors in the cortical VZ of wild-type and Nde1−/− mutant, we failed to detect a significant difference in the early S phase population but found more mutant progenitors in mid to late S phase (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by quantitative analysis of IdU-CldU labeling shown in Figure 5A.

claim: CldU signals in Nde1−/− progenitors were predominantly detected at heterochromatic domains
source: In a large number of Nde1−/− progenitors, CldU signals in IdU+CldU+ cells were predominantly detected along the nuclear periphery, the rim of nucleoli, and on particles of satellite repeats which are characteristic for heterochromatic domains, indicating replication difficulties in these domains during mid to late S phase (Figure 5B–D).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunohistological data shown in Figure 5B-D.

claim: Nde1−/− progenitors showed a reduction in the intensity and number of IdU labeled foci in PH3+ cells
source: Triple immunostaining of IdU, CldU, and PH3 allowed us to access the S to G2/M progression; we found that Nde1−/− progenitors showed a reduction in the intensity and the number of IdU labeled foci in PH3+ cells (Figure 5B, arrows), suggesting reduced nucleotide incorporation into mutant progenitors before S phase completion.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by triple immunostaining data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: DNA replication in Nde1−/− progenitors progresses normally through euchromatin but stalls during heterochromatin replication in mid-late S phase
source: Collectively, the unaltered early S phase population, significant increase in CldU labeling in various heterochromatic domains, reduced IdU labeling in PH3+ cells, combined with prolonged duration of S phase, suggest that DNA replication in Nde1−/− progenitors progresses normally through the euchromatin, but stalls during heterochromatin replication in mid-late S phase.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claim: The lengthened Ts in Nde1−/− progenitors was not mitigated by p53 removal
source: To test this hypothesis, we measured the Ts of Nde1−/−Trp53−/− progenitors and found the lengthened Ts in Nde1−/− progenitors was not mitigated by p53 removal (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by S phase duration measurement shown in Figure 6A.

claim: IdU-CldU sequential labeling indicated delayed DNA replication at heterochromatic domains in Nde1−/−Trp53−/− neural progenitors
source: Likewise, the IdU-CldU sequential labeling study also indicated delayed DNA replication at heterochromatic domains in Nde1−/−Trp53−/− neural progenitors (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by sequential labeling data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Reduced BrdU or IdU incorporation was found when Nde1−/−Trp53−/− progenitors progressed from S to G2/M
source: Reduced BrdU or IdU incorporation was found when Nde1−/−Trp53−/− progenitors progressed from S to G2/M in 1.5 hr, which was in agreement with hindered nucleotide incorporation before S phase completion (Figure 6B,C, arrows).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunohistological data shown in Figure 6B,C.

claim: A substantial number of PH3+ progenitors in Nde1−/− and Nde1−/−Trp53−/− cortices were found mislocalized basally
source: In both Nde1−/− and Nde1−/−Trp53−/− cortices, a substantial number of PH3+ progenitors were found mislocalized basally (Figure 6C,D).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunohistological data shown in Figure 6C,D.

claim: Chromosomes of mislocalized PH3+ mutant progenitors were not condensed
source: PH3 is an indicator of cells in both late-G2 and M phases; we found chromosomes of the mislocalized PH3+ mutant progenitors were not condensed (Figure 6C,D higher magnification views), indicating cell cycle arrest in G2 instead of M phase.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunohistological data shown in Figure 6C,D.

claim: Most PH3+4A4− progenitors in Nde1−/− and Nde1−/−Trp53−/− mutants were ectopically localized
source: Most PH3+4A4+ progenitors in Nde1−/− and Nde1−/−Trp53−/− mutants were correctly localized at the ventricular surface, whereas most PH3+4A4− progenitors in the mutants were ectopically localized, indicating that the basally mislocalized PH3+ cells were those arrested in late-G2 and that INM in the mutant was largely normal (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunohistological data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The level of PH3 was elevated in the Nde1−/−Trp53−/− brain
source: Consistent with the G2 arrest, we found that the level of PH3 was elevated in the Nde1−/−Trp53−/− brain (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Both Nde1−/− and Nde1−/−Trp53−/− brains showed reduced levels of Cdc25A at E12.5
source: Both Nde1−/− and Nde1−/−Trp53−/− brains showed reduced levels of Cdc25A at E12.5 (Figure 6E), supporting the notion that prolonged G2 in Nde1−/−Trp53−/− progenitors was a result of persistent DNA damage.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: None of the Nde1−/−Trp53−/− mice had altered brain structures or tumors of CNS origin
source: We followed a cohort of Nde1 Trp53 double mutant mice (n > 80) over a 4-month period, and none of the Nde1−/−Trp53−/− mice (n > 20) was found to have altered brain structures or tumors of CNS origin, though they showed obvious tumors in multiple organs outside of the CNS.
evidence: This is a primary finding from longitudinal observation of mice.

claim: Approximately one third of Nde1−/−Trp53+/− mice developed tumors predominantly of hematopoietic lineages
source: We did not find tumors in Nde1+/−Trp53+/− mice (n > 30), but approximately one third of the Nde1−/−Trp53+/− mice (∼10 out of >30) developed tumors predominantly of hematopoietic lineages including lymphoma and tumor of the thymus (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a primary finding from longitudinal observation of mice shown in Figure 6 supplement 1A.

claim: Nde1−/−Trp53+/− thymus tumors showed remarkably elevated p53 protein levels
source: Apoptosis and mitotic figures along with remarkably elevated p53 protein levels were observed in the Nde1−/−Trp53+/− thymus tumor, suggesting malignancy and increased stress in the tumor tissue (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 6 supplement 1C.

claim: Nde1 was localized in the nucleus of a subset of primary progenitors in the neocortical VZ at E12.5
source: By varying conditions of immunodetection, we found Nde1 was localized in the nucleus of a subset of primary progenitors identified by Pax6 immunoreactivity in the neocortical VZ at E12.5 (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunohistological data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: GFP-tagged Nde1 showed nuclear targeting in HeLa cells
source: The possible nuclear targeting of Nde1 was confirmed by transfecting and examining GFP-tagged Nde1 in HeLa cells using confocal microscopy (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The nuclear pool of Nde1 was elevated when progenitors were undergoing DNA replication
source: Furthermore, co-immunostaining of Nde1 and Pcna, a DNA polymerase accessory factor which marks the replication fork with a distinctive punctate pattern, indicated that the nuclear pool of Nde1 was elevated when the progenitors were undergoing DNA replication (Figure 7C), which suggested that Nde1 may translocate into the nucleus during S phase to play a direct role in DNA replication.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunohistological data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Smc3 was identified as a novel Nde1 partner from a yeast two-hybrid screen
source: To further assess the involvement of Nde1 in DNA replication, we searched for Nde1 binding proteins and identified structural maintenance of chromosomes 3 (Smc3) as a novel Nde1 partner from an Nde1 yeast two-hybrid screen.
evidence: This is a primary finding from a yeast two-hybrid screen.

claim: The physical interaction of Nde1 and Smc3 was confirmed by co-immunoprecipitation
source: The physical interaction of Nde1 and Smc3 was confirmed by the co-immunoprecipiation studies (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Smc1 and Rad21 were detected in the Nde1–Smc3 immunocomplex
source: Two other core subunits of the cohesin complex, Smc1 and Rad21, were also detected in the Nde1–Smc3 immunocomplex, indicating the direct interaction of Nde1 with the entire cohesin complex.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by co-immunoprecipitation data.

claim: The Nde1 binding domain of Smc3 corresponds to amino acids R746 to R903
source: This Nde1 binding domain of Smc3 (NBD), which corresponds to amino acids R746 to R903 in the coiled-coil region between the C-terminal globular and central hinge domains of Smc3, was immunoprecipitated and found to form a specific immunocomplex with Nde1 (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Over-expression of the NBD arrested the cell cycle preferentially in S phase
source: To determine the functional significance of the Nde1–Smc3 interaction, we over-expressed the NBD to block the binding of Nde1 with cohesin and found that NBD arrested the cell cycle preferentially in S phase (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: Many cells expressing the NBD showed fragmented nuclei or committed to apoptosis
source: We also noted that many cells expressing the NBD showed fragmented nuclei or committed to apoptosis as seen in Nde1 mutant neural progenitors (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7 supplement 1.

claim: SNF2h was consistently found in the Nde1–cohesin immunoprecipitates
source: The chromatin remodeler SNF2h was consistently found in the Nde1–cohesin immunoprecipitates (Figure 7G).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 7G.

claim: SNF2h is an ATPase chromatin remodeler that interacts with RAD21
source: SNF2h is an ATPase chromatin remodeler that interacts with RAD21 (Hakimi et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation to support it.

claim: During S phase, SNF2h is recruited to replication foci and facilitates heterochromatic remodeling
source: During S phase, SNF2h is recruited to the replication foci and facilitates heterochromatic remodeling (Zhou et al., 2009; Guetg et al., 2010; Sugimoto et al., 2011; Postepska-Igielska et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to support it.

claim: Nde1 mutation led to increased genomic instability in MEFs
source: Karyotyping analysis of mouse embryonic fibroblast (MEFs) also revealed that Nde1 mutation led to increased genomic instability similar to those that have been seen in cohesinopathy, and that Nde1 Trp53 double mutation accelerated the aneuploidy caused by the Nde1−/− single mutation.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by karyotyping data.

claim: At passage 3, more than 50% of Nde1−/−Trp53−/− MEFs were aneuploid
source: At passage 3, when Nde1−/− MEFs only showed a modest increase in aneuploidy compared to the wild-type MEFs, more than 50% of the Nde1−/−Trp53−/− MEFs were aneuploid.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by karyotyping data.

claim: About 70% of Nde1−/− MEFs became aneuploid by passage 10
source: About 70% of the Nde1−/− MEFs became aneuploid by passage 10, but a similar degree of aneuploidy developed in the Nde1−/−Trp53−/− MEFs at passage 5 (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by karyotyping data shown in Figure 7 supplement 2A.

claim: More severe chromosomal aberrations were frequently observed in Nde1−/−Trp53−/− MEFs compared to Nde1−/− MEFs
source: While some Nde1−/− cells showed chromosomal aberrations with visible chromosome breaks on crossed chromosome arms, which was reminiscent of what have been observed in cohesin mutants (Peters et al., 2008), more severe chromosomal aberrations including breaks, fragmentation, detachments, and cross of chromosome arms were frequently observed in Nde1−/−Trp53−/− MEFs (Figure 7—figure supplement 2B,C).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by karyotyping data shown in Figure 7 supplement 2B,C.

claim: Cohesin is an essential guardian of genome integrity
source: Smc3 is a core subunit of cohesin, an essential guardian of genome integrity.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Cohesin forms a ring-like structure to embrace chromatin fibers from replication fork until onset of anaphase
source: Composed of SMC1, SMC3, SCC1 (RAD21), and SCC3 (STAG), cohesin forms a ring-like structure to embrace chromatin fibers from the moment they arise following the replication fork until the onset of anaphase to ensure the proper segregation of genetic materials to daughter cells (Nasmyth, 2011).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation to support it.

claim: Heterochromatin constitutes a significant portion of the mammalian genome
source: Heterochromatin constitutes a significant portion of the mammalian genome and is preferentially formed at chromosomal regions with high density of repetitive DNA elements, such as rRNA genes, centromeres, pericentromeres, and telomeres (Lander et al., 2001; Grewal and Jia, 2007; Politz et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to support it.

claim: Heterochromatin produces RNA transcripts necessary for establishment of heterochromatic states
source: However, heterochromatin is known to produce RNA transcripts necessary for the establishment of heterochromatic states (Bierhoff et al., 2014), and these RNA transcripts were preferentially generated during the replication of the heterochromatin in late S phase (Li et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to support it.

claim: Repetitive sequences of heterochromatin are hotspots for recombination
source: Heterochromatin may not only influence gene expression profiles through regulating the higher-order chromatin structure, the repetitive sequences of heterochromatin are also hotspots for recombination which represent serious challenges to genomic integrity (Peng and Karpen, 2008; Almouzni and Probst, 2011).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to support it.

claim: TG1 progressively increases over fourfold in mice from E11 to E17
source: In addition to the S phase, previous observation has shown that neocortical neurogenesis is governed by the length of G1 phase of the cell cycle (TG1) (Lange et al., 2009; Pilaz et al., 2009), which progressively increases over fourfold in mice from E11 to E17 (Takahashi et al., 1995; Miyama et al., 1997).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to support it.

claim: Over 30,000 replication origins are unutilized in each mammalian cell cycle
source: In mammalian cells, over 30,000 origins are unutilized in each cell cycle; the spatiotemporal pattern of replication origin activation may depend on, as well as determine, a cell's differentiation state (Gilbert, 2010; Nordman and Orr-Weaver, 2012; Rhind and Gilbert, 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to support it.

claim: The peak of S phase defect in Nde1 mutants at E12 to E13 overlaps with the period when Ts is at top value and TG1 increased most drastically
source: As the peak of S phase defect in Nde1 mutants at E12 to E13 overlaps with the developmental period, when Ts is at the top value and TG1 increased most drastically (Takahashi et al., 1995; Miyama et al., 1997), it is not unreasonable to speculate that the early phase of neuronal fate determination involves the reprogramming of chromatin state that initiates in G1 and executes in S phases.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on temporal correlation of observations.

claim: The core Nde1 protein is approximately 40 kDa
source: The core Nde1 protein is approximately 40 kDa and comprises an N-terminal extended coiled-coil that shows remarkable evolutionary conservation.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the protein structure.

claim: Nde1 is primarily expressed in neural progenitors and hematopoietic cells
source: However, Nde1 is diverged structurally and functionally from its paralog Ndel1 in mammals outside of the coiled-coil and is primarily expressed in neural progenitors and hematopoietic cells (Feng et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation to support it.

claim: The native Nde1 protein in developing mouse tissue is very insoluble and exists at a relatively low level
source: We have found that the native Nde1 protein in the developing mouse tissue is very insoluble and exists at a relatively low level, but genetic studies have shown that Nde1/NDE1 is an essential player for various pivotal aspects of the neural progenitor biology.
evidence: This is a primary observation from the study.

claim: The integrity of centric/pericentric heterochromatic domains is essential for recruitment and establishment of kinetochore complexes
source: Replication forks in Nde1 mutant neural progenitors are paused or stalled at heterochromatic domains composed of centric/pericentric repeats. The integrity of centric/pericentric heterochromatic domains is essential not only for defining the chromatin state but also for the recruitment and the establishment of kinetochore complexes required for mitotic spindle formation and chromosome segregation in mitosis (Ishii et al., 2008; DeLuca and Musacchio, 2012; Mankouri et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to support it.

claim: The loss of NDE1 impairs the developing CNS much more profoundly than the hematopoietic system and other non-CNS tissues
source: It is intriguing that the loss of NDE1 impairs the developing CNS much more profoundly than the hematopoietic system and other non-CNS tissues, though NDE1 mutations are associated with leukemogenesis (Cavazzini et al., 2009; Van der Reijden et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as an observation with citations to support the leukemogenesis association.

claim: The role of NDE1 is more essential in humans than in mice
source: In the developing CNS, the role of NDE1 is more essential in humans than in mice.
evidence: This is stated as an observation based on phenotypic differences.

claim: Patients who lose both functional copies of NDE1 show severe malformation of many brain structures
source: Patients who lose both functional copies of NDE1 show severe malformation of many brain structures, but the detectable brain anatomical defect of Nde1−/− mice is largely limited to the neocortex and specifically to layer II/III cortical neurons (Feng and Walsh, 2004; Alkuraya et al., 2011; Bakircioglu et al., 2011; Guven et al., 2012; Paciorkowski et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to support it.

claim: The cerebral cortex is the largest organ in terms of both cell number and functional diversity
source: The cerebral cortex is the largest organ in terms of both cell number and functional diversity, and cortical layer II/III is expanded exponentially in evolution (DeFelipe et al., 2002; Molnar et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to support it.

claim: Somatic mutations, especially CNVs, are specifically abundant in human neurons
source: With the advent of comprehensive genome-wide analysis, somatic mutations, especially copy number variants (CNVs) are found to be specifically abundant in human neurons and increasingly linked to neurodevelopmental diseases (Grayton et al., 2012; McConnell et al., 2013; Moreno-De-Luca et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to support it.

claim: The NDE1 gene is one of the 'hot spots' for CNVs at chromosome 16p13.11
source: The NDE1 gene is one of the 'hot spots' for CNVs at chromosome 16p13.11, of which deletions and duplications have been found to associate with a wide spectrum of developmental brain disorders including intellectual disability, epilepsy, autism, schizophrenia, and attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) (Hebebrand et al., 1994; Gillberg, 1998; Sharp et al., 2006; Ullmann et al., 2007; Hannes et al., 2009; Heinzen et al., 2010; Mefford et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to support it.

claim: The genomic region spanning 16p13.11 encodes eight transcripts including NDE1
source: The genomic region span 16p13.11 encodes eight transcripts including MPV17L, C16orf45, KIAA0430, MYH11, C16orf63, ABCC1, and ABCC6 in addition to NDE1.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the genomic region.

claim: Among genes at 16p13.11, NDE1 is the only gene known to be important for brain formation
source: Among these NDE1 is the only gene that is known to be important for brain formation.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: NDE1 dosage alteration may result in secondary genomic lesions in cortical neurons
source: Findings described in this study suggest that NDE1 dosage alteration may result in secondary genomic lesions in cortical neurons.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the findings of the study.
